Q3698094.summary: This gold Latin cross, about 22.5 cm high, with gently flaring arms, is studded with a symmetrical pattern of blue and white stones and pearls set in beaded collars, and hung with six gold pendants on fine chains. A masterpiece of Lombard goldsmiths' work, it honours the Cross of Christ as a jewelled sign of victory rather than as an instrument of suffering.
facts: It is traditionally associated with the Lombard king Agilulf (d. 616), husband of Queen Theodelinda, and may have hung from a royal crown.
Its overall form and the arrangement of six pendants are Byzantine in style, while the decoration shows 'barbarian' influence, suggesting it was made within the Lombard kingdom.
Q3698094.notes: No figure of Christ is visible in the available photograph: the cross is decorated with gems and pearls. Italian Wikipedia and Wikidata state that it bears representations of Christ, archangels and apostles (presumably on engraved stones), but this could not be confirmed, so the entry is kept as uncertain; if the claim cannot be substantiated it should be removed as a non-figural cross. The Commons file description wrongly calls it a 'diptych of Gregory the Great'.

Q109422137.summary: This narrow ivory strip tells the night of Christ's betrayal in three scenes. At the top a servant-girl points accusingly at Peter in the courtyard of the high priest; in the middle Peter sits weeping, head in hand, with the cock perched before him; at the bottom the haloed Christ is led away between soldiers toward Pilate. The juxtaposition sets Peter's human weakness beside Christ's calm acceptance of his Passion.
facts: It is a side panel from a five-part ivory leaf, of the kind assembled around a larger central plaque.
The Louvre bought it in 1895 from the collector Charles Mannheim.
The cock recalls Christ's prophecy that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed.
Q109422137.notes: The Louvre identifies the lowest scene as Christ led to Pilate (Wikidata/Commons title: 'arrest of Christ'). Date and Ravenna attribution are given by the Louvre with a query, on stylistic grounds.
Q109422137.original_title: Plaque latérale d'un feuillet en cinq parties : Le Reniement de saint Pierre ; le Christ emmené chez Pilate

cur:manuscripts2-menologion-adoration-ma.summary: Before a dark cave in a rocky landscape the Virgin sits holding the Christ child on her lap, and an angel with a staff leads the three Magi, in Persian caps and rich garments, who come forward bearing their gifts. The miniature, set into the text for the feast, shows the Macedonian painters' gift for graceful movement.
facts: The Menologion of Basil II, made at Constantinople for Emperor Basil II (976–1025), holds about 430 miniatures by eight painters whose names — among them Pantoleon, Michael of Blachernai and Nestor — are written beside each image.
It covers only the first half of the church year, September to February, and passed through the hands of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, before Pope Paul V received it for the Vatican Library.
cur:manuscripts2-menologion-adoration-ma.notes: Another Commons file ('Adoration of the Magi (Menologion of Basil II).jpg') reproduces the same miniature at lower resolution.

cur:monumental-mustair-harrowing-of-hell.summary: Christ, haloed and striding forward, reaches down to grasp the hand of a figure rising from the underworld, while other haloed figures look on at the right. Like the contemporary mosaic in Santa Prassede in Rome, it shows the new importance of the Anastasis image in the West around 800.
facts: The abbey of Saint John at Müstair, founded c. 780, preserves wall paintings of about 800 arranged in five registers: the life of David at the top, three rows on the youth, ministry and Passion of Christ, and below them scenes of Saint Andrew, joined on the west wall by a Last Judgment.
UNESCO, which inscribed the abbey in 1983, describes them as Switzerland's greatest series of figurative murals, painted around 800.

vam:O316627.summary: Drawn in sure black outlines with washes of red, a young figure with a cap of curly hair and a large halo stands frontally, one hand grasping a tall staff, his tunic and mantle edged with red bands. The V&A describes him as Christ the Good Shepherd. The cloth is torn, and no sheep survives, though a red shape at the right edge hints at the lost part of the composition.
facts: The V&A's brief record describes the piece as Egyptian, of the 600s, painted in red, blue and black.
The Good Shepherd, a young man carrying or guarding his flock, is one of the oldest ways in which Christians pictured Christ, drawing on his words in John 10 (general context).
vam:O316627.notes: The museum record is minimal (no description beyond 'Christ as Good Shepherd'). The haloed figure with a staff is consistent with the identification, but no sheep or inscription is visible, so the identification rests on the museum title.

walters:W.185.72V.summary: Christ hangs on the cross beneath a titulus, his thin pale body bleeding from his wounds and his head bowed, against a patterned ground of gold and blue. The Virgin, wrapped in a deep blue mantle, stands at the left with her hand to her face, and John, in red, holds a book at the right. The miniature is set in a wide margin of gold ivy sprays.
facts: The book was probably made for a married couple who were originally painted kneeling with scrolls and coats of arms in the margins flanking this Crucifixion; their figures and arms were later erased and overpainted with white.
The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.
walters:W.185.72V.notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

Q136029633.summary: Christ and the apostles gather around a long table beneath red drapery, but the central platter holds what is usually identified as a roasted cuy (guinea pig), a traditional Andean festive dish, alongside local fruits and foods. Marcos Zapata, a leading Andean painter of the Cusco School, translated the European Last Supper into the visual and culinary world of the Peruvian highlands. The painting remains one of the best-loved images in Cusco Cathedral and a vivid emblem of Andean Christianity.
facts: Guinea pigs had long been raised and eaten in the Andes and used as sacrificial animals on ritual occasions, so the dish gave the sacred meal a familiar, festive meaning for local viewers; some scholars suggest the animal may instead be a viscacha.
Zapata ran a large, productive workshop in Cusco, painting at least 200 works between 1748 and 1764, including some fifty large canvases on the Litany of Loreto for the cathedral.
The Cusco School combined European compositions, often copied from Flemish prints, with Andean flora, fauna and abundant gold ornament.

Local tradition holds that Judas was given the features of the conquistador Francisco Pizarro, and guides often describe the drink on the table as chicha — popular stories rather than documented facts.
